item.title: The patient safety divide: When cyber threats become clinical hazards
item.description:
Walk into any modern hospital, and the convergence of physical care and digital infrastructure is everywhere. From smart HVAC systems maintaining negative pressure in isolation wards to internet-connected infusion pumps and robotic surgical assistants, modern healthcare is powered by an ecosystem of connected care devices.

For years, healthcare cybersecurity has been dominated by a singular narrative: protecting electronic health records (EHR) and complying with HIPAA. But as clinical environments become hyperconnected, the attack surface has fundamentally shifted. Today, when a hospital network is breached, it isn’t just data that is compromised. Patient safety, operational continuity, and clinical care delivery are all threatened.

The numbers are a wake-up call. According to Claroty’s 2026 global survey on operational resilience, 52% of healthcare organizations experienced a cybersecurity incident that impacted their cyber-physical systems (CPS) or operational environment in the past 12 months.

The financial toll of these attacks is significant, with each incident averaging $923,706 in losses, including one-third of the incidents exceeding half a million dollars. But the real story lies in the physical fallout. For healthcare leaders, the traditional IT security playbook is no longer sufficient. It is time to bridge the gap between digital security and operational resilience.

Here is what the latest data tells us about the state of operational resilience in healthcare and why closing the patient safety divide must become a top executive priority.

Healthcare system downtime increases patient risk

In traditional IT, a breach means stolen data or regulatory fines; in healthcare OT, a breach compromises clinical uptime and patient safety. While the financial consequences were real for the organizations that faced cyber incidents in the past 12 months, it was operational downtime (44%) and safety incidents/hazards (40%) that had the biggest impact, outstripping financial loss (28%) and reputational damage (28%) as leading impacts.

For those incidents that resulted in downtime, 34% of downtime incidents lasted between one day and two weeks. In an operating room, ICU, or diagnostics lab, 24 hours of downtime is not an IT inconvenience but rather a disruption to patient admissions, surgical schedules, and emergency care delivery.

Healthcare OT security investments must address growing threats

Globally across all 16 industries in the survey, ransomware was cited as a top threat to operations by only 27% of leaders. In healthcare, that number jumps to 35%, trailing only IT-to-operational spillover (37%) and AI-powered attacks (36%). Despite the physical operational risk, security budgets remain heavily skewed toward enterprise IT: 38% of organizations dedicate over 40% of their cybersecurity spend exclusively to IT systems. In contrast, 40% spend 20% or less on securing CPS/OT, and 12% spend less than 10%.

Attackers routinely pivot from traditional IT into operational and medical networks through lateral movement, but organizations are still underinvesting in the endpoint and network protections required to secure medical devices and OT assets. Protecting patient safety, not just personal data, should be at the forefront of cybersecurity investment.

Healthcare cyber resilience hinges on bridging IT-OT divide

When there’s an IT vs. OT disconnect in responsibility and accountability ahead of cyber incidents, imagine the scramble and fallout that can take place during one. This “readiness” gap can have severe consequences for patients.

Only 13% of healthcare organizations report that IT and CPS security governance are fully integrated (lagging the global cross-industry average of 16%). This gap creates verified patient risk. IT and clinical engineering must operate under a shared model of clear accountability where risk ownership is transparent and remediation is non-negotiable.

And while 74% claim a proactive or structured compliance approach, their No. 1 operational barrier to achieving compliance is IT/OT alignment challenges (32%), followed by third-party risk (26%) and legacy proprietary systems that cannot be patched (23%). The takeaway here is that passing compliance audits on paper does not equal clinical resilience when the teams managing clinical engineering, hospital operations, and IT security operate in functional silos.

For CIOs focused on operational resilience and taking organizational steps to protect patient safety, understanding the very real risks of asset downtime, the growing OT threat landscape, and the IT-OT divide is a good place to start. Explore the full extent of Claroty’s global research to see how risk to physical operations is impacting how organizations across the global regions and industries are responding to the latest threats.

item.title: AI needs $4.2 trillion in new revenue. Which industries could create it?
item.description:
The billions flowing into chips, data centers, networks, and power systems have focused attention on the challenge of the AI buildout. But the more important question, according to Bain & Company’s Technology Report 2026, may be whether that buildout will produce economic value to justify it.

How much revenue does AI need to pay for itself?

Capital expenditures in the arms race among hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle) could reach $780 billion in 2026. That’s almost five times the level of just three years earlier.

By 2031, spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion a year, including new data center infrastructure and compute capacity as well as ongoing upgrades to the installed base of GPUs, memory, and networking equipment.

If we assume that capital expenditures amount to about 25% of industry revenue (an ambitious but reasonable percentage based on trends among cloud providers), sustaining this level of investment would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion annually.

Where some of that revenue will come from is increasingly clear. Enterprise adoption could contribute $1 trillion to $1.4 trillion to providers alone as AI delivers meaningful productivity gains to enterprises across software development, sales, marketing, customer service, and IT operations. And consumer AI products, through subscriptions and advertising, could generate an estimated $200 billion to $400 billion by 2031. Together, those enterprise and consumer AI markets could total between $1.2 trillion and $1.8 trillion.

But that still leaves about $4.2 trillion of new revenue to reach the $6 trillion market that Bain estimates will be necessary to fund the buildout (see Figure 1). That revenue must come from new sources of economic value.

Figure 1

What does AI’s funding gap mean for non-tech companies?

The $4.2 trillion gap won’t be filled by the technology industry alone. Much of it is likely to come from value created across healthcare, manufacturing, mobility, energy, and other sectors.

Enterprise productivity is the first of the gains we’re seeing from AI deployment, but it won’t be nearly enough. The economics required to generate ROI from AI infrastructure are demanding trillions in new revenue, not just cost savings. The industry needs a wave of application innovation comparable with what mobile and cloud unlocked.

For CEOs outside the tech world, that wave is the part to watch. AI companies need new revenue and will have to build for new customers. The new products and capabilities that result could change how non-tech companies compete. Leaders who begin building conviction now about what that means for their industry will be better positioned to win in that future.

Which business opportunities could fill the gap?

Bain’s research finds that four key categories of innovation are most likely to help deliver the growth needed to support the buildout.

  1. Autonomous everything ($400 billion): Automakers, logistics companies, and industrial operators could use AI to autonomously operate automobiles, trucks, drones, and other industrial equipment, tapping a $400 billion market opportunity by increasing equipment uptime while reducing training and operating costs.
  2. Physical AI ($900 billion): Advanced AI models can enable highly realistic simulations and digital twins of physical processes, helping manufacturers and other industrial companies improve productivity. Similarly, AI-powered robotics, including humanoid robots, can operate in unstructured environments, unlocking a wide range of new applications across the physical economy, from manufacturing to surgery. As a result, the physical economy could represent a $900 billion opportunity across priority sectors (including automotive, electronics, semiconductors, and aerospace and defense), assuming a 10% reduction in R&D and manufacturing costs.
  3. New product development: Beyond AI’s uses today, companies in healthcare, materials, energy, and scientific research could build new products and services that help close the gap. These could include AI-driven drug discovery that makes treatments for rare diseases economically viable, always-available mental health support, materials science breakthroughs that unlock next-generation batteries and semiconductors, and autonomous scientific research that accelerates progress in fields from neuroscience to fusion energy.
  4. Search and advertising: For brands and marketers, AI chatbots that are increasingly replacing much of traditional internet search could become a new advertising channel to reach customers.

These categories reach across the economy, and the winners will be the companies that create breakthrough applications that transform industries. For CEOs outside tech, the question becomes: Where could AI create a new revenue pool in your industry?

Read the full analysis in Bain & Company’s Technology Report 2026.

item.title: Do legacy systems wear out?
item.description:
As I staggered into the computer room at three in the morning, I saw the look of fear on the operator’s face. The system was down again: not the first time this month. This legacy IBM mainframe was beginning to look like my stepfather’s car. I wondered: do legacy systems just wear out?

Old hardware

Let me tell you about my stepfather Tony and his car. The first time I sat in the passenger seat, I looked down and saw a steel plate welded to the floor, covering a hole that had rusted through. Water pipes poked up by the windscreen blowing hot air (when the heater worked), and as we sped along at an impressive 35 miles per hour, you could hardly talk from the sound of wind whistling through gaps. Not a comfortable driving experience. One more thing: it often broke down.

Experts talk about the ‘bathtub curve’ showing how things like computer equipment may fail early in their life from manufacturing defects, then have a stable period before the chance of failure increases with age. Tony’s car was an excellent demonstration of this, as old parts failed. This is what I faced as I entered the computer room.

The disk subsystem had failed, and everything else crashed as a result. At 3 am, this older disk subsystem looked like a bad idea.

Keep old hardware running

My Uncle Bill is around the same age as Tony and has a mint-condition Series 1 Land Rover. If you’re not a Land Rover fan, these were released in the late 1940s and 1950s: far older than Tony’s rust-bucket. But Bill’s car still hums along today.

Just like Bill’s Land Rover, older computing equipment is still in use: sometimes in critical areas. Germany’s train operator Deutsche Bahn made headlines in 2024 when it was found to rely on a Windows operating system not supported since 2001. In 2025, the FAA admitted to using equipment up to 50 years old.

Like Bill, the company I worked for kept this old hardware running by relying on support from an external vendor. This vendor performed regular maintenance and used hardware features to monitor its operation and predict failures. Although it didn’t predict my failure, the vendor provided 24/7 support. When the disk failed, the support engineer figured out the problem, found and obtained replacement parts, and installed them.

Vendors will often support hardware for years. For example, Apple stops supporting its devices 7 years after they are last sold. In my area of mainframes, IBM stops supporting its mainframe hardware 6-7 years after they are ‘end of marketing.’ Ideally, hardware is replaced before this time.

Rather than rely on external support, another option is to keep staff on site that can fix the hardware, together with spare hardware, or a cache of spare parts. In emergencies, like the FAA, they may resort to eBay.

Following Bill’s practices can keep older hardware running, and many do. But there was still an outage when my disk subsystem failed.

Critical systems like those in aircraft use redundancy to cope with this: multiple components doing the same job. If one fails, others keep running.

So, older hardware systems don’t wear out; individual components do. But what about software?

Software rot

Software isn’t made up of anything physical: there are no transistors to fail, no power supplies to catch fire. So, can a bunch of bytes wear out?

On 14-Oct-2025, Microsoft ended support of Windows 10. This doesn’t mean that Windows 10 stopped working on this date. Rather, Microsoft stopped providing fixes for Windows. However, StatCounter claims that 25% of all Windows users still use Windows 10, and some rely on even older versions.

As explained by the US Cyber Defense Agency, regularly updating software with patches and fixes is important to maximize security, with other possible benefits including performance improvements. In my mainframe world, knowing a vendor will guarantee their software works, and fix it if it doesn’t, is just as important. In fact, software support can be brilliant. One client had a critical system that failed to reboot in the middle of the night. The vendor had a fix shipped within hours.

As with hardware, vendors may end support. They may end support for a specific version like Windows 10, often providing an upgrade path to a new version. Or, like Broadcom, they may retire a product altogether. My clients should upgrade or retire software before support ends, though some don’t get there.

Bytes may not wear out, but software can face new problems not predicted when first developed. The Y2K problem is a great example: software storing the year as 2 digits in the 1990s would have problems come 2000. Vendors fixed supported products and guaranteed they would work after the year 2000. Note carefully the word ‘supported’: no one is fixing unsupported software.

Dates aren’t the only issue. Another client needed to double workloads to be processed by a suite of applications. Substantial changes were needed to their legacy COBOL software. Fortunately, they had staff supporting this software that could make these changes.

Some software may rely on other libraries, software, or standards. In May 2026, TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 were deprecated. Software using these versions must be updated to provide acceptable security. Tony faced this when the government made retractable seat belts in cars mandatory. The solution for everyone is the same: those supporting the software must retrofit the required technology.

This doesn’t mean that all old software is ready to fail. In 1991 IBM released the most recent version of their Document Composition Facility (DCF) software. IBM still supports it, and I see clients happily using it today.

Storage

In my case, the disk subsystem had a storage medium failure: the disk crashed. Once the part was replaced, I restored data from backups on tape. But if disks can fail, can’t tape? Or any storage medium: flash drives, CDs?

The Library of Congress found that CDs last for over 30 years, a period matched by tape manufacturers like Fujifilm. But these figures assume the media is stored in correct conditions: Bill stores his Land Rover in a garage away from direct sunlight and dust.

Disk drives don’t last as long: Backblaze and SANDisk showed hard and solid-state disk drives failing from 3-10 years. Enterprise disk subsystems and cloud providers manage this with redundancy features. But anyone with an old single disk drive may be in trouble.

These figures will differ depending on the manufacturer, operating environment, and frequency of usage. Anyone subscribing to Tony’s maintenance ethos and buying cheaper or used parts will get what they pay for. But storage media needs the same attention as hardware and software: management, maintenance, and support.

Maintenance and care

The company I worked for looked after their systems well: hardware and software. They had support, installed updates, and stored storage media correctly. They followed Bill’s lead.

The computer systems were moved to a new data center, and the disks began to fail. The hardware vendor recommended replacing components for all disks, even though there was no immediate evidence they would fail. My company decided that the extra money and outages were not worth it. They leaned towards Tony’s methods and paid the price.

Legacy systems don’t wear out. Poorly maintained, managed or supported legacy systems do.

item.title: Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson Airport shows where physical AI can create value
item.description:
Seven thousand cameras ought to make it pretty hard to lose someone in an airport. But imagine being the person who has to find him. All you know is that he is tall, wearing a red hat and a blue jacket, and someone has reported that he dropped a bag and ran. Somewhere in that enormous collection of camera feeds is the information you need. Meanwhile, he is moving.

Chris Crist, the chief information officer at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), used that example in a conversation with our research team. A red hat and a blue jacket is actually a pretty decent description if you happen to be watching the right camera. With the computer vision software Crist and his team have added to part of the airport’s camera network, a security professional can use those details to search across feeds. Enter “red hat” and “blue jacket,” and the AI returns potential matches within seconds. The security professional reviews them, selects the person who fits the description and can then see the live feeds where that person appears.

According to Crist, the security team reported that average response times fell by 75% for most incidents it handled using the software. Think about how far the man in the red hat could get while someone is still looking for him on a monitor. This is a very different conversation about productivity from the one we have about finishing a presentation faster.

Physical AI turns existing infrastructure into an operational advantage

It also helps explain why physical AI deserves attention beyond the robotics demonstrations. Robots tend to command our attention, but AI’s ability to interpret a physical environment can change the work of the people already responsible for it. At Atlanta’s airport, the security professional still evaluates the match and determines the response. The technology takes on the exhausting search through footage that stands between an initial report and an informed decision. The airport had already invested in the ability to see. AI is now helping its people make use of what those cameras capture. Crist described overlays across nearly 2,000 cameras which gives his team a substantial operating environment in which to learn, while leaving room to expand across the wider network. “It’s in a production state. We’re seeing the results. We’re already thinking about other use cases,” he told our team.

We appreciate that combination of ambition and willingness to work through the details. Especially because some of those details turned out to be very hot. The new system needed computing equipment with GPUs that used more power and generated more heat than the team had planned for. They put it into an existing technology room, the room overheated, and outages followed. “We ended up having to distribute them across multiple IDFs in our facility to distribute the heat appropriately,” Crist said, referring to the airport’s technology rooms. You can have a compelling AI strategy and still find yourself stopped by the cooling capacity of a room.

Taking physical AI beyond security

Once the team got the system running reliably, Crist was able to start asking what else it might help people at the airport find. A wheelchair when a passenger needs one, for instance. That got us thinking about who else might have a question for a camera originally installed for security.

Consider a retailer that wants to know whether a new display is working. Sales data tells the team what sold. AI can analyze the camera feeds to identify patterns that would take employees hours of observation to piece together: how many shoppers pass the display, how many stop and how long they stay. Combined with sales data, that analysis could help the merchandising team see whether a display attracts attention but rarely leads to a purchase, or whether customers spend time in a department where help is often unavailable. The team can then change the display, move an associate or test a different layout and use the AI to see whether the change makes a difference. It cannot tell you why someone did not buy, but it can help you decide where to investigate.

A hotel could use the same approach to understand why check-in goes smoothly on some afternoons and leaves guests waiting on others. AI could analyze activity across the lobby over time, showing when queues build and how long they take to clear. Combined with arrival forecasts and staffing schedules, those patterns could help managers anticipate when another check-in position will be needed. An alert when a queue starts growing could also give the team time to respond before the lobby fills with frustrated guests. As in the store, the team could make a change and measure whether it helps.

Of course, opening another check-in position will only help if staffing is the problem. A guest services manager may recognize that a recurring delay has more to do with rooms not being ready than with too few people checking guests in. A store associate may know why shoppers linger at a display without buying. I would want those people working with the technology team from the beginning, helping decide what the AI should look for and what they could do with what it finds. They bring the context needed to turn an observation into a useful response.

At ATL, Crist’s team is exploring whether AI could flag wheelchairs that have collected in the wrong place. The people who move chairs between gates could help the team decide when to send an alert. A row of chairs at one gate might be exactly what’s needed for an arriving flight. The question is whether a passenger at another gate is still waiting for one.

On a separate effort to improve international arrivals, Crist had a chance to measure the wait himself. He told our team his badge could have gotten him past the line, but he stayed and timed it. “I thought we can do better than this,” he said. The airport worked with U.S. Customs and Border Protection and other stakeholders to introduce biometric processing technology. Crist reported that processing time fell 54% within 30 days of its introduction in June 2025.

Start with a measurable problem—and the people closest to it

This is a good starting point for innovation. Spend enough time inside the experience you are responsible for, and the problem becomes harder to accept. It also becomes much easier to explain to the people whose help you need. There was a wait to shorten and a result the team could measure. That is a useful discipline to carry into the next round of AI investments.

For the camera initiative, security provided that initial focus. “In our case, we started with using it for security purposes,” Crist said. His team’s next challenge is deciding which of the other opportunities deserves investment. We would ask the people proposing each application to be equally clear about the result they expect. If AI helps locate equipment, who will retrieve it and how much time could that save? If it reveals a recurring bottleneck, can the team change the staffing or layout that contributes to it? Those questions help establish whether an observation is something the business can act on and whether doing so is worth the investment.

Defining the problem clearly also helps determine how much information the application actually needs. A retailer may need to know how many people stop at a display without needing to know who they are. A hotel can study congestion in public areas without extending observation into private guest spaces. Deciding what information is actually needed, who can use it and how long to keep it should be part of designing the application.

As these applications develop, some of the responses may eventually be carried out by machines. Crist’s team is considering how intelligence from the physical environment might guide autonomous wheelchairs, vehicles and other systems. That would take the work beyond helping a person find something or recognize a problem to helping a machine navigate the airport and perform a task. It fits within his longer-term ambition for a journey with far less friction between the entrance and the gate.

Leaders do not have to wait for that future to begin exploring what physical AI could do in their own organizations. Start by asking the people running a store, a hotel or an airport what they repeatedly struggle to see or respond to in time. Then bring them together with the technology team to work through whether AI could help. Give them responsibility for testing the idea and improving the result together.

At ATL, the cameras were already there. The first opportunity was to help someone find the person in the red hat before he disappeared from view. Having made that work, Crist and his colleagues have good reason to look at what else they might be missing.

item.title: 3 ways digital leaders manage AI-enabled data source proliferation
item.description:
Companies have spent years collecting data, hoping to use it one day. That time has now come, and AI is helping digital leaders untangle and sort the glut of enterprise information. Cutting-edge tech is also creating new data sources that power decision-making processes.

Getting to this point hasn’t been easy. For many years, CIOs and their peers focused their data analysis on quantitative sources. Structured data powered business intelligence systems, while technological limitations made it difficult to process unstructured sources. Qualitative sources were very much the untapped companion to their structured equivalents.

However, AI has changed that relationship, reports Forrester. Companies can use AI to process unstructured data, such as images, text, video, and behavioral signals, alongside structured information to create new insights, operational efficiencies, and customer experiences.

New tech also helps create new data. Professionals can use gen AI services like ChatGPT and Claude to produce new content sources. The Pew Research Center found signs of AI authorship in over one-third of internet pages published after ChatGPT’s release in late 2022.

Agents are another source of information. Gartner reports that agentic AI applications in the physical world produce vast amounts of data as they interact. The tech analyst suggests AI agents will generate 10 times more data from physical environments than all digital AI applications combined by 2029.

But even with all the data they’ve collected and continue to bring into the business through AI services, organizations sometimes need more. Gartner further reports an increasing proportion of firms use AI to fill gaps in real-world data sources. The analyst says 75% of businesses will use gen AI to create synthetic customer data this year, up from under 5% in 2023.

The evidence shows that digital leaders must oversee an ever-increasing range of information across structured and unstructured data sources, and that’s a challenge. Smart digital leaders who manage the proliferation of data in the AI age focus on these three key areas.

1. Curate information effectively

Emmanuel Frenehard, CDO at biopharmaceutical giant Sanofi, is one executive helping his organization exploit its information. His team oversees a range of initiatives, including those involving synthetic data.

“AI can generate very meaningful, useful insights for us,” he says. “In our world, where patient data is rare, you can generate data to test your models. With rare diseases, you can touch thousands of patients around the globe. Sometimes that data is almost impossible to find. We can now create synthetic data to simulate situations.”

All use cases go through an approval process. For large-scale explorations, Frenehard discusses options with Sanofi’s AI board and the CFO. “I make sure we connect the dots so we don’t create proliferation,” he says, explaining how the firm scales its disparate efforts, from generative to agentic AI, across 80 countries.

Rather than letting people deploy their own agents, Sanofi has built its AI-powered Concierge service to help employees exploit data assets, using Snowflake as the data foundation for governance and collaboration. As many as 65,000 of the firm’s 80,000-plus employees already use Concierge monthly across a range of business functions and activities.

“I think we need to be cautious about the proliferation of chatbots and other AI services,” says Frenehard. “What I tell my team is we don’t want a new legacy. Most digital leaders inherited a legacy. We don’t want to create someone else’s with AI, so strict data governance is super important.”

Tim Chilton, a managing geospatial consultant at UK mapping agency Ordnance Survey (OS), is another executive who doesn’t want today’s AI efforts to create tomorrow’s data headaches. He says it’s crucial to curate information effectively, which his team upholds by combining human-in-the-loop governance with trusted data platforms.

“This approach means continuing our principle of creating a master version of our data sets and then recognizing that there are many destinations that those data sets will need to go to, and that’s all in the efficiency of the architecture we build,” he says.

The data architecture he and his team are building is about creating data sets once and then sharing them to these platforms, hopefully with open standards where people can be more responsive. “It means if these pockets of curated data pop up, OS can redirect itself and get our data into those platforms and curated data stores quite quickly,” he says.

2. Build business confidence

Gill Haus, CIO at Chase, the consumer banking arm of JPMorgan Chase & Co, agrees that human judgment is the key to unlocking value from a proliferation of AI-enabled data sources. Emerging technology can help people sift information and produce insights rapidly. However, speedy outcomes aren’t necessarily the right ones.

“If I make a decision using the wrong data, I’ll likely make the wrong decision,” he says. “What’s important for an organization is to have great data hygiene, data products, confidence, and access, and restrictions on the information, as well as to ensure that any technology, whether an agent, traditional AI, or just an application with access to data, is governed well. Then you can have confidence in the output.”

Chase has spent many years exploring AI and ML, and through these efforts, they’ve learned that governance creates confidence. “That’s the part we focus on getting right,” he says. “Because if I’m going to make an underwriting or a fraud decision, it must be right. I need to make sure I have that same level of confidence when I’m using data for agents.”

Francois-Xavier Pierrel, group chief data and ad tech officer at French TV network TF1, says everything his organization does with data is aligned with a business unit. One example is an audience graph, or Graph ID, which provides a structure for all TF1’s logged-in accounts. The broadcast giant has about 25 million profiles with around 100 criteria. Each profile includes key data points like name, email, device, connections, and tastes.

“We defined the audience graph with the advertising and streaming teams,” he says, referring to the technology’s development. “We set the criteria for each profile and how information is used for each use case. That approach gives us control because we’re collecting millions of hits a year on the platform.”

Pierrel says TF1 has used Graph ID to set the parameters for its data transformation efforts, including agentic explorations. The firm launched an agent to help sales staff find insights last summer. They’re also exploring how they can reduce the strain on data analysts by automating daily reporting. Across these efforts, Graph ID is the gold standard for data.

“Everything goes as raw data into Azure,” he says. “From there, we put it into Snowflake. And from Snowflake, we have a bronze, silver, and gold model, and everybody works on the gold model. But that model is defined together with the business unit so we’re sure we can guarantee lineage, reliability, quality, and scalability.”

3. Set the right context

The key message for digital leaders, Workday’s VP of AI platform Dean Arnold says, is with the right data foundations in place, professionals can now pull information from multiple sources more quickly and in new combinations to generate insights. However, they must consider how they’ll proactively oversee this process.

“Being able to manage data creation over time, certainly as a semantic layer, is going to be a challenge,” he says. “There’s this great expansion of what we can do and what’s available, and we must consider how we govern, control, and look at the datasets, and understand who owns them and who has access to them. You need that auditability all the way down.”

Arnold’s colleague, CIO Rani Johnson, says the enterprise data and analytics team helps professionals across the business understand AI’s significance. “They’re helping us figure out how to prioritize what data to value and how to value data differently with the right context,” she says.

Johnson adds that Workday has an effective master data management system and a series of technologies that classify information. “We’ve got a thoughtful data strategy,” she says. “It’s all about ensuring we’re not dirtying the lake with things that don’t have relevance.”

That sentiment chimes with Loïc Giraud, VP of data and AI at healthcare and pharmaceutical company Novo. While digital leaders must manage more information sources than before, good data management practices are still key to success.

“To some extent, I don’t think this process has changed,” he says. “The volume has, but the process remains the same. The things we try to push are to make sure the data that’s being produced is being catalogued and made easily accessible for us to consume.”

The vital element to emphasize, suggests Josh Chandler, CDIO at Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, is AI is just another tool in the data management kit bag. While emerging tech can help professionals source and sort information, it’s far from a complete solution to all business data challenges, despite the hyperbole.

“The reality is you’ve still got to get your house in order,” he says. “That’s often the thing people don’t want to hear. It’s the hard graft around data, and the thing that doesn’t sound particularly attractive. But it’s still necessary because it remains to be seen whether all the promises of AI will be realized.”

item.title: I built an AI agent. It broke my assumptions about my own team
item.description:
As a CTO, I’ve found that building AI automations gives me a better understanding of what I’m asking my team to do.

I’ve spent the past year building four iterations of an AI agent designed to route customer issues to the right engineering team. The first used Claude Code with an MCP connector to Jira. I’d hand it an issue and a prompt, and it would tell me who should look at it. For the second, I turned that workflow into an agent in n8n, a low-code framework. The third ran on Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic’s hosted agent platform. But I wanted it to have access to tools and data that the environment couldn’t reach. For the fourth, I rebuilt the agent on Google’s agent platform, where we run our production infrastructure. That gave it access to our codebase and issue tracker. I hadn’t anticipated how much data access would influence my platform of choice. As Grant Gross reports, data access and integration can be barriers to deploying agents.

Across each iteration, I kept asking whether the agent justified the work of building it. How often did it route an issue correctly? What did it cost to run? How much manual routing did it remove? Those questions gave me a way to evaluate the experiment.

The biggest surprise was discovering how much the routing process relied on knowledge our managers couldn’t fully articulate. Building the agent forced me to work through those decisions myself, giving me a better understanding of what I ask my team to do.

Here’s what I learned:

Understand the workflow before you automate

On paper, the workflow for my agent seemed ripe for automation. While our customer support team handles 90% of customer issues themselves, 10% involve product problems that require escalation to engineering. Routing those escalations was a bottleneck. Roughly 100 times a week, someone had to apply substantial domain knowledge to identify the right engineering manager.

Bernard Aceituno has similarly described successful agentic ticket-triage deployments that categorize issues and update the ticketing system. Given that my core problem was classification, I started with a simple mapping of product areas to engineering managers: this manager owns reports, this one owns the front end, this one owns administrative functions. But knowing the product area wasn’t always enough to route the ticket to the right team.

A reporting issue, for example, could have different causes. In some cases, an incorrect report indicated a front-end problem; in others, it indicated a data problem. Data ingestion belonged to one team unless the data came from an HRIS system, which another team handled. Even after the agent identified the right team, the person responsible could vary by request. My agent needed rules for both team ownership and individual assignment.

I couldn’t have asked any of the managers to write the complete set of routing rules upfront. But they could review a routing decision and say, “I would have sent it to this person for this reason.” Building the agent meant turning the group’s fragmented judgment into explicit rules.

Test whether the output is correct

The first version of the routing agent assigned only about 60% of issues correctly. It also made people up — hallucinating names, combining first and last names from different people. Engineering managers flagged incorrect assignments in Jira and explained which team or person should have received each ticket. I used those corrections to update the routing rules. Through that review process, the agent reached about 95% routing accuracy.

Checking the model’s behavior is another part of validation. Separate testing by our department showed how differently models can interpret the same restrictions. We tested OpenAI, Google and Anthropic models under rules that included a prohibition on giving employment recommendations. Gemini would go out of its way not to answer questions it felt crossed a line we had specified. Opus would get excessively creative trying to find ways to answer without violating the premise, while Sonnet followed the restriction more literally.

A new model release or even a new model family, such as a move from Claude Opus to GPT-6 or Gemini 4, can change those response patterns even when the surrounding tools and instructions stay the same. The same prompts, MCP connectors and guardrails can produce different tool-call behavior, formatting and refusals once the underlying model changes. That’s why validation needs to continue after deployment, particularly when the underlying model changes.

Decide where the automation should stop

The routing agent started with a specific job: given a problem description, what team owns that domain? And who’s the manager? But identifying the team raised other questions the agent might help answer.

I also built tools to ask: is this a regression — did a recent change cause it? Can I find the area of code where the problem lives? Do I know which developer touches that area? Together with routing, those capabilities made four tools that could be useful in sprint planning, product evaluations or other contexts. George Bezerra argues for choosing among rules, machine learning, LLMs and agents based on the problem. Building those extra capabilities made me question how much machinery my original routing task needed.

The agent also explains its assignments in Jira: “I’m a bot, and I assigned this here for these reasons.” Anyone can put a thumbs down on it. The system captures that feedback, but it does not automatically learn from each correction. I stopped short of building that capability because each additional refinement saved less time. Managers redirect the remaining ~5% of incorrect assignments, just as they did before the agent existed.

Measure whether the system removes work

I started with a concrete metric to improve: how much time engineering managers were spending in the Jira project before and after the agent went live.

The agent now saves each of our seven engineering managers about 2 hours a week. Most issues now reach the right team immediately, reducing time to resolution. Another positive data point: when the agent broke for a week, several managers came to me, noticing the manual work had come back.

What surprised me was how small the actual operational cost of the agent is: pennies a month. That figure excludes the time I spent building and refining the agent, which matters when evaluating the total investment. But I had expected higher ongoing model costs.

Ongoing maintenance is another factor in ROI calculation. The routing rules reflect our current team structure, ownership boundaries and exceptions. When one team’s responsibilities changed, we had to adjust the routing rules.

Before building another agent, I need to ask: is this a fairly static workflow, or is the team or process going to change substantially? That changes the ROI calculation significantly.

Building an agent changed my process

I suspect by next year I’ll have multiple agents running to take over tasks for our team. Some I may purchase rather than build. Building this one gave me a better basis for evaluating either option.

Whether I build or buy, I’ll want to understand how an agent handles exceptions, adapts to workflow changes and justifies the effort required to maintain it. Low operating costs mean little if the system needs constant intervention to stay useful.

While the workflow required more investigation and iteration than I expected, the operating cost turned out to be much lower. Buying an agent raises some of the same questions. I can imagine agents that are durable through organizational changes. But I can also imagine a lot that aren’t. How are those delivered? As a service? As a toolkit I plug together? As a product that just works? These are the kinds of questions I’ll be asking.

I encourage other technology leaders to build an agent themselves. Documenting the workflow, investigating incorrect results and deciding whether another improvement is worth the effort gave me a clearer understanding of automation’s true cost and value — and of the work my team does every day.

item.title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
item.description:
AWS has raised the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes in all commercial regions, with no opt-in and no new pricing. The limit had stood since 2018. AWS's post lists the costs: twice the concurrency at the same request rate, three-hour SQS visibility timeouts, and Kafka mappings that must be recreated. Practitioners welcome it and ask what belongs elsewhere.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI
item.description:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks.

By Robert Krzaczyński
